sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

[MATH: (1)/(2)\log_{2} (4x^{4}) + \log_{2} x|= 1; \log_{2} ((4x^{4})^{1/2}) + \log_{2} x|= 1; \log_{2} (2x^{2}) + \log_{2} x|= 1]

Next, we combine the logarithms using the product rule. This gives

[MATH: \log_{2} (2x^{2} ⋅ x)|= 1; \log_{2} (2x^{3})|= 1.]

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

[MATH: 2^{\log_{2} (2x^{3})}|= 2^{1}; 2x^{3}|= 2.]

Now, we solve this equation for [MATH: x] using the usual methods.

[MATH: x^{3}|= 1; root(x^{3}, 3)|= root(1, 3); x|= 1]

Let's now check for an extraneous solution by substituting back into the original equation:

Substituting [MATH: x=1] back into the original equation, we get

[MATH: (1)/(2)\log_{2} (4 ⋅ 1^{4}) + \log_{2} 1|=^(?)1; (1)/(2)\log_{2} 4 + \log_{2} 1|=^(?)1; (1)/(2)\log_{2} 4 + 0|=^(?)1; \log_{2} (4^{1/2})|=^(?)1; \log_{2} (2)|=^(?)1; 1|= 1.✓] Therefore, [MATH: x=1] is a valid solution.

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

[MATH: \log_{2} (4x) − 2\log_{2} (x^{2}) = 1; \log_{2} (4x) − \log_{2} ((x^{2})^{2}) = 1; \log_{2} (4x) − \log_{2} (x^{4})|= 1]

Next, we combine the logarithms using the quotient rule. This gives

[MATH: \log_{2} ((4x)/(x^{4}))|= 1; \log_{2} ((4)/(x^{3}))|= 1.]

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

[MATH: (4)/(x^{3})|= 2^{1}; (4)/(x^{3})|= 2.]

Now, we solve this rational equation for [MATH: x] using the usual methods.

[MATH: (4)/(x^{3})|= 2; x^{3} ⋅ (4)/(x^{3})|= x^{3} ⋅ 2; x^{3} ⋅ (4)/(x^{3})|= 2x^{3}; 2x^{3}|= 4; x^{3}|= 2; x|= root(2, 3)]

Let's now check for an extraneous solution by substituting back into the original equation:

Substituting [MATH: x=\sqrt[3]{2}] back into the original equation, we get

[MATH: \log_{2} (4(root(2, 3))) − 2\log_{2} ((root(2, 3))^{2})|=^(?)1; \log_{2} (4(root(2, 3))) − \log_{2} ((root(2, 3))^{2})^{2}|=^(?)1; \log_{2} (4(root(2, 3))) − \log_{2} ((root(2, 3))^{4})|=^(?)1; \log_{2} (4(root(2, 3))) − \log_{2} (2(root(2, 3)))|=^(?)1; \log_{2} ((4root(2, 3))/(2root(2, 3)))|=^(?)1; \log_{2} ((4root(2, 3))/(2root(2, 3)))|=^(?)1; \log_{2} ((4)/(2))|=^(?)1; \log_{2} (2)|=^(?)1; 1|= 1.✓]

Therefore, [MATH: x=\sqrt[3]{2}] is a valid solution.

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

[MATH: 2\log_{3} (sqrt(2)x) − \log_{3} (x − 1)|= \log_{3} (3x); \log_{3} (sqrt(2)x)^{2} − \log_{3} (x − 1)|= \log_{3} (3x); \log_{3} (2x^{2}) − \log_{3} (x − 1)|= \log_{3} (3x)]

Next, we combine the logarithms on the left-hand side using the quotient rule:

[MATH: \log_{3} ((2x^{2})/(x − 1))|= \log_{3} (3x)]

Now, we solve the equation for [MATH: x] using the usual methods.

[MATH: (2x^{2})/(x − 1)|= 3x; (x − 1) ⋅ (2x^{2})/(x − 1)|= (x − 1) ⋅ (3x); (x − 1) ⋅ (2x^{2})/(x − 1)|= (x − 1) ⋅ (3x); 2x^{2}|= 3x^{2} − 3x; x^{2} − 3x|= 0; x(x − 3)|= 0]

So, [MATH: x = 0] and [MATH: x =3.]

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting them back into the original equation:

  • Substituting [MATH: x=0] back into the original equation, we get [MATH: 2\log_{3} (sqrt(2) ⋅ 0) − \log_{3} (0 − 1)|=^(?)\log_{3} (3 ⋅ 0); 2\log_{3} (0) − \log_{3} (− 1)|=^(?)\log_{3} (0).×] This statement is false because [MATH: \log_3 (0)] and [MATH: \log_3 (-1)] are undefined. Therefore, [MATH: x=0] is not a valid solution.

  • Substituting [MATH: x=3] back into the original equation, we get [MATH: 2\log_{3} (3sqrt(2)) − \log_{3} (3 − 1)|=^(?)\log_{3} (3 ⋅ 3); \log_{3} (3sqrt(2))^{2} − \log_{3} (2)|=^(?)\log_{3} (9); \log_{3} (18) − \log_{3} (2)|=^(?)\log_{3} (9); \log_{3} ((18)/(2))|=^(?)\log_{3} (9); \log_{3} (9)|= \log_{3} (9).✓] Therefore, [MATH: x=3] is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: x=3] only".
